claim: Telomerase synthesizes chromosome-capping telomeric repeats using an active site in telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) and an integral RNA subunit template.
source: Telomerase synthesizes chromosome-capping telomeric repeats using an active site in telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) and an integral RNA subunit template.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about telomerase function, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: Telomerase reconstitutions yielded heterogeneous DNA-bound TERT monomer and dimer complexes in relative amounts that varied with assembly and purification method.
source: Surprisingly, telomerase reconstitutions yielded heterogeneous DNA-bound TERT monomer and dimer complexes in relative amounts that varied with assembly and purification method.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-molecule imaging experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Cellular holoenzyme and minimal recombinant enzyme monomeric for TERT had catalytic activity.
source: Among the complexes, cellular holoenzyme and minimal recombinant enzyme monomeric for TERT had catalytic activity.
evidence: This is supported by activity-dependent elution experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Dimerization was suppressed by removing a TERT domain linker with atypical sequence bias.
source: Dimerization was suppressed by removing a TERT domain linker with atypical sequence bias, which did not inhibit cellular or minimal enzyme assembly or activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with TERT-ΔPAL and TERT-20N constructs shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Removing the TERT domain linker did not inhibit cellular or minimal enzyme assembly or activity.
source: Dimerization was suppressed by removing a TERT domain linker with atypical sequence bias, which did not inhibit cellular or minimal enzyme assembly or activity.
evidence: Activity assays in Figure 6 show that PAL-deleted TERT maintains catalytic activity.

claim: Human telomerase establishes conserved telomerase subunit architecture from single-celled organisms to humans.
source: Overall, this work defines human telomerase DNA binding and synthesis properties at single-molecule level and establishes conserved telomerase subunit architecture from single-celled organisms to humans.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that human telomerase, like ciliate and yeast telomerases, functions as a TERT monomer.

claim: Insufficient telomere synthesis ultimately compromises telomere function and signals a halt to cell proliferation.
source: Insufficient telomere synthesis ultimately compromises telomere function and signals a halt to cell proliferation (O'Sullivan and Karlseder, 2010; Aubert, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Telomere-linked restriction of cellular renewal leads to failures of highly proliferative human tissues, with clinical manifestations including bone marrow failure, aplastic anemia, and pulmonary fibrosis.
source: This telomere-linked restriction of cellular renewal leads to failures of highly proliferative human tissues, with clinical manifestations including bone marrow failure, aplastic anemia, and pulmonary fibrosis (Armanios and Blackburn, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior clinical research.

claim: The active human telomerase ribonucleoprotein (RNP) includes telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), which provides the active site, and an RNA (hTR) containing a reiteratively copied internal template.
source: The active human telomerase ribonucleoprotein (RNP) includes telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), which provides the active site, and an RNA (hTR) containing a reiteratively copied internal template.
evidence: This is established knowledge about telomerase composition.

claim: The TERT N-terminal (TEN) domain allows retention of single-stranded DNA during the template repositioning required for tandem repeat synthesis.
source: The TERT N-terminal (TEN) domain allows retention of single-stranded DNA during the template repositioning required for tandem repeat synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TEN domain function.

claim: TEN-domain-truncated TERT supports only single-repeat synthesis that can be complemented to high repeat addition processivity by the TEN domain as a separate polypeptide.
source: TEN-domain-truncated TERT, designated 'TERT ring' based on Tribolium TERT structure (Gillis et al., 2008), supports only single-repeat synthesis that can be complemented to high repeat addition processivity by the TEN domain as a separate polypeptide (Robart and Collins, 2011; Wu and Collins, 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: A biologically functional human telomerase holoenzyme contains two sets of H/ACA proteins (dyskerin, NHP2, NOP10, and GAR1) bound to hTR to direct RNP biogenesis and TCAB1 to redistribute the RNP from nucleoli to Cajal bodies.
source: In addition to these and other catalytic activity requirements for TERT and hTR, a biologically functional human telomerase holoenzyme contains two sets of H/ACA proteins (dyskerin, NHP2, NOP10, and GAR1) bound to hTR to direct RNP biogenesis and TCAB1 to redistribute the RNP from nucleoli to Cajal bodies (Egan and Collins, 2012a; Podlevsky and Chen, 2012; Schmidt and Cech, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on telomerase holoenzyme composition.

claim: Telomerase holoenzyme must assemble with the shelterin protein TPP1 for telomere recruitment and extension of chromosome ends.
source: Telomerase holoenzyme must also assemble with the shelterin protein TPP1 for telomere recruitment and extension of chromosome ends (Lue et al., 2013; Nandakumar and Cech, 2013; Sexton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The number of TERT-hTR complexes per cell is estimated as only ∼35 or ∼250 in even the most highly telomerase-positive tumor cell lines.
source: Endogenous human telomerase is scarce, with the number of TERT-hTR complexes per cell estimated as only ∼35 (Cohen et al., 2007) or ∼250 (Xi and Cech, 2014) in even the most highly telomerase-positive tumor cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior quantification studies.

claim: Human telomerase enzymes reconstituted in cells or in RRL can interact with the same length of single-stranded DNA and have similar specific activity.
source: Importantly, human telomerase enzymes reconstituted in cells or in RRL can interact with the same length of single-stranded DNA, have similar specific activity, and have only minor differences in other enzyme properties such as repeat addition processivity (Jurczyluk et al., 2010; Zaug et al., 2013; Wu and Collins, 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior comparative studies.

claim: RNP affinity purification and structural studies indicate a single RNA and single TERT per biologically functional telomerase holoenzyme of single-celled eukaryotes.
source: RNP affinity purification and structural studies indicate a single RNA and single TERT per biologically functional telomerase holoenzyme of single-celled eukaryotes (Livengood et al., 2002; Witkin and Collins, 2004; Cunningham and Collins, 2005; Hong et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2013; Bajon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The minimal Tetrahymena telomerase RNP assembled in RRL has a subunit stoichiometry of single RNA and single TERT.
source: This subunit stoichiometry is recapitulated by the minimal Tetrahymena telomerase RNP assembled in RRL (Bryan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Some assays suggest TERT and hTR function as monomeric subunits, without dominant-negative inhibition of a wild-type subunit by co-expressed mutant subunit.
source: However, the subunit stoichiometry of an active human telomerase RNP is unresolved: some assays suggest TERT and hTR function as monomeric subunits, without dominant-negative inhibition of a wild-type (WT) subunit by co-expressed mutant subunit (Errington et al., 2008; Egan and Collins, 2010), while other assays suggest obligate co-dependence of active site function across TERT and hTR subunits (Wenz et al., 2001; Sauerwald et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies showing lack of dominant-negative effects.

claim: Other assays suggest obligate co-dependence of active site function across TERT and hTR subunits.
source: However, the subunit stoichiometry of an active human telomerase RNP is unresolved: some assays suggest TERT and hTR function as monomeric subunits, without dominant-negative inhibition of a wild-type (WT) subunit by co-expressed mutant subunit (Errington et al., 2008; Egan and Collins, 2010), while other assays suggest obligate co-dependence of active site function across TERT and hTR subunits (Wenz et al., 2001; Sauerwald et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies suggesting TERT dimerization.

claim: Analysis using single-molecule fluorescence correlation spectroscopy detected one TERT and one hTR per RRL-reconstituted minimal RNP.
source: Analysis using single-molecule fluorescence correlation spectroscopy detected one TERT and one hTR per RRL-reconstituted minimal RNP (Alves et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior single-molecule study.

claim: Cellular subunit overexpression, purification, and crosslinking yielded particles observed by electron microscopy that were proposed to be active dimeric TERT RNPs, based on detection of two bound single-stranded DNAs.
source: On the other hand, cellular subunit overexpression, purification, and crosslinking yielded particles observed by electron microscopy that were proposed to be active dimeric TERT RNPs, based on detection of two bound single-stranded DNAs (Sauerwald et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior electron microscopy study.

claim: ACP and ACP-based tags are well suited to single-molecule labeling applications because they are small, monomeric, and expose the conjugated prosthetic group as a conformationally dynamic extension from the protein surface.
source: ACP and ACP-based tags are well suited to the applications developed here because they are small, monomeric, and expose the conjugated prosthetic group as a conformationally dynamic extension from the protein surface (Byers and Gong, 2007; Chan and Vogel, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ACP tag properties.

claim: Human TERT tagged at the N-terminus supports telomere elongation, whereas telomerase assembled with C-terminally tagged TERT does not.
source: Human TERT tagged at the N-terminus supports telomere elongation, whereas telomerase assembled with C-terminally tagged TERT does not (Counter et al., 1998; Wong and Collins, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on TERT tagging.

claim: ACP- and MCP-tagged TERTs expressed at equivalent level and assembled active telomerase.
source: ACP- and MCP-tagged TERTs expressed at equivalent level and assembled active telomerase, quantified by radiolabeled dGTP incorporation in reactions also containing dTTP and ddATP (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot and activity assay data in Figure 1C.

claim: CoA-Cy5 labeling of ACP-TERT using ACP synthase and CoA-Cy3 labeling of MCP-TERT using SFP synthase were confirmed by SDS-PAGE and fluorescence scanning.
source: CoA-Cy5 labeling of ACP-TERT using ACP synthase and CoA-Cy3 labeling of MCP-TERT using SFP synthase were confirmed by SDS-PAGE and fluorescence scanning, with no labeling of TERT lacking an ACP or MCP tag (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence gel data in Figure 1D.

claim: The profile of telomerase product synthesis was not affected by the labeling reaction for fluorophore conjugation.
source: Importantly, the profile of telomerase product synthesis was not affected by the labeling reaction for fluorophore conjugation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assay data in Figure 1E.

claim: O-purification by the hTR template enriched more telomerase activity relative to TERT than did F-purification.
source: O-purification by the hTR template enriched more telomerase activity relative to TERT than did F-purification (Figure 1F), as would be expected based on template hybridization vs antibody binding to TERT.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot and activity assay data in Figure 1F.

claim: Most of the TERT in 293T-F and RRL-F was not assembled as telomerase RNP.
source: Comparison between the pair of 293T or RRL purifications suggests that most of the TERT in 293T-F and RRL-F was not assembled as telomerase RNP.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of activity to TERT levels in Figure 1F.

claim: Primers with the 3′ permutation T2AG3 have exceptionally stable binding to human telomerase due to the finely tuned recognition of template-paired primer 3′ ends in the enzyme active site.
source: Primers with this 3′ permutation of the telomeric repeat have exceptionally stable binding to human telomerase (Wallweber et al., 2003) due to the finely tuned recognition of template-paired primer 3′ ends in the enzyme active site (Brown et al., 2014; Wu and Collins, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on primer binding.

claim: Optimal DNA binding by human telomerase requires a primer length of two telomeric repeats.
source: Optimal DNA binding by human telomerase requires a primer length of two telomeric repeats (Wallweber et al., 2003), which is the same length that active human telomerase protects from nuclease digestion (Wu and Collins, 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Two-color co-localization and photobleaching assays revealed the presence of more than one labeled TERT in a subset of the DNA-bound TERT complexes.
source: Both two-color co-localization and photobleaching assays revealed the presence of more than one labeled TERT in a subset of the DNA-bound TERT complexes (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-molecule imaging data in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in TERT co-localization comparing DNA-bound 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O complexes (17–23%, p = 0.58).
source: In the two-color co-localization assay, there was no statistically significant difference in TERT co-localization comparing DNA-bound 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O complexes (Figure 2A; 17–23%, p = 0.58).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of co-localization data in Figure 2A.

claim: 293T-F complexes had much more TERT co-localization (46%, p = 0.0015) compared to 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O complexes.
source: In contrast, 293T-F complexes had much more TERT co-localization (46%, p = 0.0015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of co-localization data in Figure 2A.

claim: Results from the photobleaching method indicated no statistically significant difference in TERT subunit content across the population of DNA-bound complexes from 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O (19–27% bleaching in multiple steps, p = 0.33).
source: Results from the photobleaching method of TERT subunit counting also indicated no statistically significant difference in TERT subunit content across the population of DNA-bound complexes from 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O (Figure 2B; 19–27% bleaching in multiple steps, p = 0.33).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of photobleaching data in Figure 2B.

claim: 293T-F complexes had much more multistep photobleaching (43%, p = 0.0066) including a substantial fraction of complexes that photobleached in three or even more than three steps (12%).
source: In contrast, 293T-F complexes had much more multistep photobleaching (43%, p = 0.0066) including a substantial fraction of complexes that photobleached in three or even more than three steps (12%).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of photobleaching data in Figure 2B.

claim: There is excellent correlation of two-color co-localization to two-step photobleaching results for 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O but not 293T-F.
source: There is excellent correlation of two-color co-localization to two-step photobleaching results for 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O but not 293T-F (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Labeling of 293T- and RRL-reconstituted, F-purified MCP-TERT complexes was to saturation within 30 min of a reaction with CoA-Cy3 or CoA-Cy5.
source: Labeling of 293T- and RRL-reconstituted, F-purified MCP-TERT complexes was to saturation within 30 min of a reaction with CoA-Cy3 or CoA-Cy5 (Figure 3A), well within the standard 2-hr labeling protocol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetics data in Figure 3A.

claim: Labeling efficiency was not dependent on the reconstitution and purification method.
source: Also, labeling efficiency was not dependent on the reconstitution and purification method (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of labeling across methods in Figure 3B.

claim: If RRL-reconstituted F-purified MCP-TERT was labeled to saturation with CoA-Cy3 and then labeled with CoA-biotin, no biotinylation of TERT could be detected.
source: First, we confirmed that CoA-biotin is used equivalently to CoA-fluorophore by measuring competition between CoA-biotin and CoA-Cy3. If RRL-reconstituted F-purified MCP-TERT was labeled to saturation with CoA-Cy3 and then labeled with CoA-biotin, no biotinylation of TERT could be detected (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequential labeling data in Figure 3C.

claim: Labeling with CoA-biotin drastically reduced subsequent labeling with CoA-Cy3.
source: Similarly, labeling with CoA-biotin drastically reduced subsequent labeling with CoA-Cy3 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequential labeling data in Figure 3C.

claim: Streptavidin depleted 54.9 ± 0.7% or 50.6 ± 5.9% of biotin-labeled ACP-TERT or MCP-TERT, respectively.
source: Depletion was an indistinguishable 54.9 ± 0.7% or 50.6 ± 5.9% of ACP-TERT or MCP-TERT, respectively, quantified from the unbound ∼45% or ∼49% (Figure 3D, lanes 3–6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by depletion data in Figure 3D.

claim: Streptavidin depleted 49% of the TERT protein.
source: Streptavidin depleted 49% of the TERT protein (Figure 3F), consistent with the previous TERT depletions (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 3F.

claim: 38% of biotinylated TERT remained unbound after streptavidin depletion.
source: However, 38% of biotinylated TERT remained unbound (Figure 3F), revealing that streptavidin binding in 2 M urea did not completely deplete the labeled TERT.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biotin immunoblot data in Figure 3F.

claim: The MCP-TERT-labeling efficiency was 82%.
source: Correcting the quantified total TERT depletion for depletion efficiency of biotin-TERT gives an MCP-TERT-labeling efficiency of 82% (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is calculated from depletion data in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: TERT monomer complexes exceeded TERT dimer complexes in the DNA-bound 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O populations across almost the entire range of modeled labeling efficiencies.
source: TERT monomer complexes exceeded TERT dimer complexes in the DNA-bound 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O populations across almost the entire range of modeled labeling efficiencies (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calculations based on co-localization and photobleaching data in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: TERT complexes competent for DNA binding can have a single subunit of TERT.
source: Overall, these analyses establish that TERT complexes competent for DNA binding can have a single subunit of TERT.
evidence: This is concluded from the quantification of TERT monomer content in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: Reproducibly, more elution of WT TERT complexes occurred in the presence of buffer with dTTP + dATP vs buffer alone.
source: Reproducibly, more elution of WT TERT complexes occurred in the presence of buffer with dTTP + dATP vs buffer alone (Figure 4C, compare black and gray).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity-dependent elution data in Figure 4C.

claim: D868A TERT complexes showed the same amount of dissociation with or without dNTPs.
source: In contrast, D868A TERT complexes showed the same amount of dissociation with or without dNTPs (Figure 4C, compare dark and light blue).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity-dependent elution data in Figure 4C.

claim: The fraction of WT TERT complexes with activity-dependent elution varied widely across the TERT populations from different reconstitution and purification conditions.
source: Curiously, the fraction of WT TERT complexes with activity-dependent elution varied widely across the TERT populations from different reconstitution and purification conditions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity-dependent elution data in Figure 4C.

claim: The fraction of DNA-bound 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O TERT complexes with nucleotide-dependent-'specific' elution overlaps the fraction of DNA-bound complexes with monomeric TERT.
source: Importantly, the fraction of DNA-bound 293T-O, RRL-F, and RRL-O TERT complexes with nucleotide-dependent-'specific' elution (Figure 4C) overlaps the fraction of DNA-bound complexes with monomeric TERT (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of data in Figures 3H, 3I, and 4C.

claim: The reduction of TERT spot count by activity-based elution occurred entirely in complexes with single-step photobleaching.
source: The reduction of TERT spot count by activity-based elution occurred entirely in complexes with single-step photobleaching (Figure 4E, p = 0.0006).
evidence: This is demonstrated by photobleaching quantification after elution in Figure 4E.

claim: Human telomerase catalytic activity requires only a single TERT subunit per RNP.
source: Overall, the findings above strongly suggest that human telomerase catalytic activity requires only a single TERT subunit per RNP.
evidence: This is concluded from the activity-dependent elution data showing that TERT monomers are catalytically active.

claim: Bulk 293T-F purifications of MCP-TERT contained a large amount of a proteolytic product corresponding to the MCP-tagged TERT TEN domain alone.
source: Bulk 293T-F purifications of MCP-TERT contained a large amount of a proteolytic product corresponding to the MCP-tagged TERT TEN domain alone (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SDS-PAGE analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: DNA binding across a titration from 0.3 to 30 nM DNA yielded Kd calculations in nM of 4.9 ± 0.7 for 293T-O, 5.4 ± 1.1 for 293T-F, 8.7 ± 2.0 for RRL-O, and 14.7 ± 5.4 for RRL-F.
source: DNA binding across a titration from 0.3 to 30 nM DNA yielded Kd calculations in nM of 4.9 ± 0.7 for 293T-O, 5.4 ± 1.1 for 293T-F, 8.7 ± 2.0 for RRL-O, and 14.7 ± 5.4 for RRL-F (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA binding titration data in Figure 5C.

claim: The ∼5 nM Kd of holoenzyme and ∼10 nM Kd of minimal RNP are consistent with the holoenzyme Km for elongation of similar primers measured as 2 nM or 8 nM.
source: The ∼5 nM Kd of holoenzyme and ∼10 nM Kd of minimal RNP are consistent with the holoenzyme Km for elongation of similar primers measured, under different conditions, as 2 nM or 8 nM (Wallweber et al., 2003; Jurczyluk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to prior measurements cited.

claim: DNA binding by 293T-F TERT complexes increased ∼fourfold with 100 nM compared to 30 nM DNA.
source: DNA binding by 293T-F TERT complexes increased ∼fourfold with 100 nM compared to 30 nM DNA (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA binding data in Figure 5D.

claim: 293T-O TERT complexes showed no additional DNA binding at 100 nM compared to 30 nM DNA concentration.
source: In contrast, at 100 nM compared to 30 nM DNA concentration, 293T-O TERT complexes showed no additional DNA binding and RRL-F and RRL-O complexes showed only limited additional association with DNA (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA binding data in Figure 5D.

claim: Human TERT amino acids 201–325 are 18% proline, 14% arginine, and 12% glycine.
source: Human TERT amino acids 201–325 are 18% proline, 14% arginine, and 12% glycine.
evidence: This is a compositional analysis of the TERT linker sequence.

claim: SEG analysis identified two segments of the linker, residues 213–248 and 313–323, as low complexity.
source: SEG analysis (Wootton and Federhen, 1993) to search for low-complexity sequence within the human TERT linker. SEG analysis identified two segments of the linker, residues 213–248 and 313–323, as low complexity.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis using SEG.

claim: The PAL-mutant TERT proteins expressed at levels similar to WT TERT in 293T cells and in RRL.
source: The PAL-mutant TERT proteins expressed at levels similar to WT TERT in 293T cells and in RRL (Figure 6A), and binding of WT and PAL-mutant TERT complexes to FLAG antibody resin enriched similar amounts of catalytic activity (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 6A.

claim: Binding of WT and PAL-mutant TERT complexes to FLAG antibody resin enriched similar amounts of catalytic activity.
source: The PAL-mutant TERT proteins expressed at levels similar to WT TERT in 293T cells and in RRL (Figure 6A), and binding of WT and PAL-mutant TERT complexes to FLAG antibody resin enriched similar amounts of catalytic activity (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assay data in Figure 6B.

claim: Direct fusion of the TEN domain to the TERT ring appeared to reduce the amount of the longest product DNAs.
source: Although direct fusion of the TEN domain to the TERT ring did not substantially affect the quantified overall activity it appeared to reduce the amount of the longest product DNAs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is observed in activity assay data in Figure 6B.

claim: The change in product profile from direct TEN-ring fusion was rescued by NAAIRS repeat insertion.
source: This change in product profile was rescued by NAAIRS repeat insertion (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assay data in Figure 6B.

claim: Primer extension was highly processive for complexes of WT TERT, TERT-∆PAL, and TERT-20N assembled in 293T cells.
source: Under these conditions, primer extension was highly processive for complexes of WT TERT, TERT-∆PAL, and TERT-20N assembled in 293T cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulse-chase activity assay data in Figure 6C.

claim: Human TERT linker length and linker sequence have a very limited influence on the catalytic activity of reconstituted holoenzyme or minimal RNPs.
source: We conclude that human TERT linker length and linker sequence have a very limited influence on the catalytic activity of reconstituted holoenzyme or minimal RNPs.
evidence: This is concluded from activity assays of PAL-mutant TERTs in Figure 6.

claim: Within a twofold difference, the TPP1 OB-fold domain co-purified active telomerase regardless of TERT linker length or sequence.
source: Within a twofold difference, the TPP1 OB-fold domain co-purified active telomerase regardless of TERT linker length or sequence (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-purification and activity assay data in Figure 6D.

claim: The 293T TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N bulk purification fractions lacked the TERT proteolysis products co-enriched by WT TERT.
source: Curiously, the 293T TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N bulk purification fractions lacked the TERT proteolysis products co-enriched by WT TERT (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SDS-PAGE analysis in Figure 6E.

claim: A dramatic decrease in TERT co-localization was observed for TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N relative to WT TERT (21% vs 5% co-localization in 293T samples, p = 0.0008, and 22% vs 2–3% in RRL samples, p < 0.0001).
source: A dramatic decrease in TERT co-localization was observed for TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N relative to WT TERT (Figure 7A; 21% vs 5% co-localization in 293T samples, p = 0.0008, and 22% vs 2–3% in RRL samples, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-localization data in Figure 7A.

claim: RRL-reconstituted TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N complexes were 98% and 96% TERT monomer, respectively.
source: By calculations using a value of 82% TERT-labeling efficiency, RRL-reconstituted TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N complexes were 98% and 96% TERT monomer, respectively (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is calculated from co-localization data in Figure 7B.

claim: For 293T-reconstituted TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N complexes, TERT monomers were 94% of the population with a lower-bound underestimate of 89–90%.
source: For 293T-reconstituted TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N complexes, TERT monomers were 94% of the population with a lower-bound underestimate of 89–90% (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is calculated from co-localization data in Figure 7B.

claim: MCP-tagged TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N complexes assembled in 293T cells or RRL were dramatically depleted for multistep photobleaching compared to WT TERT complexes (24% vs 8–9% multistep bleaching in 293T samples, p = 0.0036, or 22% vs 4–7% in RRL samples, p = 0.0073).
source: MCP-tagged TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N complexes assembled in 293T cells or RRL were dramatically depleted for multistep photobleaching compared to WT TERT complexes (Figure 7C; 24% vs 8–9% multistep bleaching in 293T samples, p = 0.0036, or 22% vs 4–7% in RRL samples, p = 0.0073).
evidence: This is demonstrated by photobleaching data in Figure 7C.

claim: More elution of TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N complexes occurred in buffer + dNTPs than in buffer alone.
source: To determine whether RNPs assembled with TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N retained the characteristic permutation dependence of human telomerase DNA binding, we tested Cy5-labeled MCP-tagged TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N complexes for activity-dependent elution. More elution of TERT-∆PAL and TERT-20N complexes occurred in buffer + dNTPs than in buffer alone (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity-dependent elution data in Figure 7E.

claim: PAL disruption drastically reduced TERT dimerization, but RNPs assembled with PAL-mutant TERTs retained catalytic activity and the permutation-dependent release of product DNA characteristic of the human telomerase active site.
source: We conclude that although PAL disruption drastically reduced TERT dimerization, RNPs assembled with PAL-mutant TERTs retained catalytic activity and even the permutation-dependent release of product DNA characteristic of the human telomerase active site.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data in Figure 7.

claim: TERT dimerization was as effectively suppressed for telomerase holoenzyme assembled in cells as for minimal RNP assembled in RRL.
source: TERT dimerization was as effectively suppressed for telomerase holoenzyme assembled in cells as for minimal RNP assembled in RRL, suggesting that the TERT subunit content of reconstituted complexes has no dependence on any holoenzyme protein other than TERT.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of PAL-mutant TERT data across reconstitution methods in Figure 7.

claim: Human telomerase complexes monomeric for TERT are catalytically active.
source: Whether assembled in vivo or in vitro, we show that human telomerase complexes monomeric for TERT are catalytically active.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the activity-dependent elution experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Monomeric TERT was abundant in the populations of DNA-bound complexes from at least three of the four bulk purification samples examined.
source: Monomeric TERT was abundant in the populations of DNA-bound complexes from at least three of the four bulk purification samples examined here, particularly from any purification using a template-complementary oligonucleotide.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: These results establish the phylogenetic conservation of a TERT-monomer telomerase active site.
source: These results establish the phylogenetic conservation of a TERT-monomer telomerase active site.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that human telomerase functions as a TERT monomer, like ciliate and yeast telomerases.

claim: The results support TERT haploinsufficiency rather than dominant-negative inhibition as the mechanism accounting for human disease from heterozygous TERT mutation.
source: Also, our results support TERT haploinsufficiency rather than dominant-negative inhibition as the mechanism accounting for human disease from heterozygous TERT mutation (Armanios et al., 2005; Armanios and Blackburn, 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that telomerase functions as a TERT monomer.

claim: The budding yeast telomerase holoenzyme has a TERT monomer.
